# Purpose {.unnumbered}

These notes cover the machinery paper 5 uses. They are a tutorial, not a
report: there are no results here, and nothing is claimed as new. The aim is
that a reader with undergraduate mathematics can follow what paper 5 fitted
and why the pieces are arranged as they are, or fill in the details
independently from here.

The order is cumulative. Each section uses only what precedes it. Sections 1
and 2 are standard and kept short; sections 3 and 4 are where general
machinery meets this particular likelihood, and are the point of the note.

Notation: $x \in \mathbb{R}^p$ is a feature vector for one runner in one
race, $\theta$ is the collection of all model parameters, and $\sigma(u) =
(1+e^{-u})^{-1}$.

# Neural networks

## A unit

A single unit takes an input vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^p$, forms a weighted
sum, and applies a fixed nonlinear function:

$$
a \;=\; \varphi\!\left(w^\top x + b\right), \qquad w \in \mathbb{R}^p,\;
b \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

The weights $w$ and the bias $b$ are learned; $\varphi$ is chosen in advance.
The common choice, and the one paper 5 uses, is the rectified linear unit
$\varphi(u) = \max(0, u)$.

## Layers, width, depth

A layer applies $m$ units to the same input, which is a matrix multiply
followed by an elementwise nonlinearity:

$$
h \;=\; \varphi\!\left(W x + b\right), \qquad W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p},
\; b \in \mathbb{R}^m .
$$

$m$ is the width. Layers compose: $h^{(1)} = \varphi(W_1 x + b_1)$,
$h^{(2)} = \varphi(W_2 h^{(1)} + b_2)$, and so on. The number of layers is
the depth. A network of this shape, ending in a linear map to a single
number, is a multi-layer perceptron. Paper 5's scorer has two hidden layers
of widths 256 and 128.

## Why the nonlinearity is the point

Without $\varphi$, depth buys nothing. Two stacked affine maps are one
affine map:

$$
W_2\!\left(W_1 x + b_1\right) + b_2 \;=\; \left(W_2 W_1\right) x +
\left(W_2 b_1 + b_2\right),
$$

and the same collapse holds for any number of layers. A deep linear network
has more parameters than a single linear map but represents exactly the same
set of functions. Everything a network can do beyond linear regression comes
from $\varphi$.

With $\varphi = \max(0, \cdot)$, each unit is an affine function of its input
switched on or off by a half-space test $w^\top x + b > 0$. A composition of
such units is a piecewise-linear function of $x$, and the regions on which it
is linear are determined by the weights — they are learned, not specified.
This is the concrete sense in which such a network expresses thresholds and
region-dependent behaviour, and it is what section 4 draws on.

## Universal approximation, stated honestly

A network with one hidden layer of sufficient width can approximate any
continuous function on a compact set to arbitrary accuracy. This is a
statement about existence: for a given target function and tolerance, such
weights exist.

It does not say how wide the layer must be, and the width required can grow
very quickly with the dimension of $x$. It does not say that gradient descent
will find those weights; the optimisation problem is non-convex and nothing
guarantees the global optimum is reached. And it says nothing at all about
generalisation — the theorem concerns approximating a known function, not
recovering one from a finite, noisy sample. It is a reason not to worry that
the model class is too small. It is not a reason to expect a good fit.

# Training

## The loss and gradient descent

Fitting means choosing $\theta$ to minimise a scalar loss $L(\theta)$
computed from the data. The basic method is gradient descent: repeatedly
step against the gradient,

$$
\theta \;\leftarrow\; \theta - \eta \, \nabla_\theta L(\theta),
$$

with step size $\eta$, the learning rate. Too large and the iterates
oscillate or diverge; too small and progress is slow.

## Backpropagation

The gradient is obtained by the chain rule. Write the network as a
composition $L = \ell \circ f_n \circ \cdots \circ f_1$. The chain rule gives
the derivative of $L$ with respect to the parameters of layer $i$ as a
product of Jacobians of the layers above it. Evaluating that product from the
loss end downward — reverse mode — lets every layer reuse the partial product
already computed by the layers above, so the whole gradient costs a small
constant multiple of one forward evaluation. That is backpropagation: not a
separate idea from the chain rule, but the efficient order in which to apply
it.

## Automatic differentiation, and what an unbroken chain means

The framework does not differentiate symbolically. It records each operation
as it executes, building a graph from the parameters to the scalar loss, and
then walks that graph backwards applying each operation's known derivative.

"An unbroken differentiable chain from the loss" is a concrete requirement on
that graph, and it fails in ordinary ways:

- **Leaving the graph.** Converting a tensor to a plain number, or to an
  array outside the framework, and continuing the computation there. The
  recorded graph ends at that point and everything upstream receives no
  gradient.
- **Operations with no derivative.** Rounding, comparison, sorting to
  produce an index, casting to an integer type. These have zero or undefined
  derivative almost everywhere; a parameter reached only through one of them
  cannot be trained.
- **Selection that still differentiates both sides.** An elementwise
  conditional such as `where(condition, a, b)` returns the value of one
  branch, but its backward pass computes derivatives for both. If the
  discarded branch contains a non-finite value — $\log 0$, a division by zero
  — the forward result is correct and the gradient is `NaN`. This is worth
  knowing because a check on the loss value alone will not detect it. The
  remedy is to make the discarded branch finite before the selection rather
  than relying on the selection to remove it.

## Optimisers, epochs, minibatches

Plain gradient descent uses the whole dataset for each step. Stochastic
gradient descent uses a random subset — a minibatch — giving a noisier
gradient at a fraction of the cost. One pass over the training data is an
epoch.

Adam is the optimiser paper 5 uses. It keeps running averages of the gradient
and of its elementwise square, and scales each parameter's step by the ratio
of the two, so parameters with consistently small gradients take relatively
larger steps. It has its own learning rate, which remains the most important
setting.

Weight decay adds $\lambda \lVert \theta \rVert^2$ to the loss, shrinking
parameters toward zero. Dropout, used during training only, sets a random
fraction of a layer's activations to zero at each step, which discourages the
network from relying on any single unit.

## Overfitting, and why a validation slice exists

A network with many parameters can fit the training data closely and still
predict badly. The symptom is a training loss that keeps falling while the
loss on data not used for fitting rises.

This creates a problem for every choice not made by gradient descent — width,
depth, learning rate, dropout rate, how many epochs to train. Those cannot be
selected on the training loss, which prefers more capacity and more epochs
without limit. They also cannot be selected on the data reserved for the
final estimate of performance: a quantity chosen to look good on a particular
set is no longer an unbiased estimate of performance on that set.

The resolution is a third partition. The data is split into a fitting set, a
validation set used to make those choices and to decide when to stop, and a
test set that is scored once at the end and is otherwise not consulted. Paper
5 carves its validation slice out of the training period by date, so that no
information from later races reaches an earlier fit.

# The Plackett–Luce likelihood under a neural scorer

## The likelihood

Papers 2b and 3 derive this likelihood; it is unchanged here, and the only
difference is what computes the score.

Consider race $r$ with $J_r$ runners. Each runner $j$ has features $x_{rj}$
and receives a score

$$
z_{rj} \;=\; f_\theta\!\left(x_{rj}\right) \in \mathbb{R},
$$

where $f_\theta$ is any function with parameters $\theta$ — a linear map, a
tree ensemble, or a network. The Plackett–Luce model says that the horse
finishing first is drawn from the field with probability proportional to
$\exp(z)$; that the second is drawn from the remainder by the same rule; and
so on. Truncating at depth $k$, and writing $(s)$ for the horse that finished
$s$-th and $R_{r,s}$ for the set still unplaced at stage $s$,

$$
\Pr\!\left(\text{observed top-}k\text{ order in race } r\right)
\;=\;
\prod_{s=1}^{S_r} \frac{\exp\!\left(z_{r,(s)}\right)}
{\sum_{j \in R_{r,s}} \exp\!\left(z_{rj}\right)},
\qquad S_r = \min\!\left(k, J_r - 1\right).
$$

The loss is the negative log-likelihood, summed over races:

$$
L(\theta) \;=\; \sum_r \ell_r, \qquad
\ell_r \;=\; -\sum_{s=1}^{S_r}\left[\, z_{r,(s)} \;-\;
\log \!\!\sum_{j \in R_{r,s}} \!\! \exp\!\left(z_{rj}\right) \right].
$$

At $k = 1$ this is the conditional logit: only the winner enters, and each
race contributes one softmax term. Paper 5 uses $k = 3$, as papers 2b and 3
do.

## What the gradient hands to the network

Differentiating $\ell_r$ with respect to a single score gives, for runner $j$,

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_r}{\partial z_{rj}}
\;=\; \sum_{s=1}^{S_r} \left( p_{rj}^{(s)} - \mathbb{1}\!\left\{j = (s)\right\}
\right),
\qquad
p_{rj}^{(s)} \;=\;
\frac{\exp(z_{rj})}{\sum_{i \in R_{r,s}} \exp(z_{ri})}
$$

for $j \in R_{r,s}$, and $p_{rj}^{(s)} = 0$ once $j$ has been placed and
removed. The quantity is "predicted probability minus what happened",
accumulated over the stages the runner survives to.

This is the entire interface between the likelihood and the model. The
likelihood produces one number per runner-row; backpropagation carries that
number into $f_\theta$ by the chain rule. Nothing in the derivation depends
on $f_\theta$ being linear, which is why the same objective serves paper 2b's
linear predictor, paper 3's tree ensemble and paper 5's network without
modification.

## Race as the grouping unit

Two structural facts follow from the form of the likelihood.

**Only within-race differences matter.** Adding a constant $c_r$ to every
score in race $r$ leaves every ratio unchanged:
$\exp(z + c_r) / \sum \exp(z + c_r) = \exp(z)/\sum \exp(z)$. The scorer is
therefore identified only up to a per-race constant. Numerically this is also
useful: subtracting $\max_j z_{rj}$ before exponentiating prevents overflow
without changing the result.

**Runners are coupled only through the denominator.** The score $z_{rj}$
depends on $x_{rj}$ alone. Runners in the same race interact only through the
normalising sum. Runners in different races do not interact at all.

## Shared weights and variable field sizes

The same $f_\theta$ is applied to every runner. The model has no parameter
attached to "the second runner" or "the favourite"; it is a function of one
runner's features, evaluated once per row. Two consequences:

- The model is equivariant to permuting the runners within a race. Reordering
  the rows reorders the scores and leaves the likelihood unchanged.
- Field size requires no architectural provision. A function
  $\mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}$ is indifferent to how many rows it is applied
  to.

The complication is arithmetic, not architectural. Evaluating many races at
once is efficient if the scores are held in a rectangular array, but races
have different field sizes. The usual solution is to pad each race to the
width of the widest race in the batch and carry masks that record what is
real:

- a **validity** mask marking real runners against padded entries, so padding
  contributes nothing to any sum; and
- a **stage** mask recording, for each stage $s$, which runners are still in
  $R_{r,s}$.

Both masks must be applied so that padded entries contribute neither a value
nor a gradient — which is the concrete case of the conditional-selection
hazard described in section 2.3.

# What an MLP can represent that a linear score cannot

This section is specific to the likelihood above. The interesting differences
are not the textbook ones about function classes in general; they follow from
scoring being race-conditional.

## The linear case

With $f_\theta(x) = \beta^\top x$, the comparison between two runners in the
same race is

$$
z_j - z_i \;=\; \beta^\top\!\left(x_j - x_i\right).
$$

The model's opinion about any pair is a fixed linear functional of their
feature difference. It is the same functional everywhere in feature space and
for every race.

## Interactions must be named

Suppose the value of a low draw depends on the course and the distance —
worth a great deal over five furlongs at one track, worth nothing over twelve
at another. A linear score can express this only if the product of draw and
course, or draw and distance, is supplied as its own column. Papers 1 and 2
did exactly that, with an explicit course-by-draw interaction.

The requirement is that every interaction be anticipated, constructed and
named in advance. There are $\binom{p}{2}$ pairwise products and far more
higher-order ones, so in practice a small number are chosen on prior belief.

A network needs none of them. Each hidden unit tests a half-space
$w^\top x + b > 0$; the composition produces functions that are linear on
regions and different from one region to the next. The effective slope on any
feature can therefore depend on the values of the others. This is not a
guarantee that the network finds the right interaction, only that the model
class contains it without it having been named.

## Thresholds and saturation

In a linear score the marginal effect of a feature is constant: one more day
since the last run changes $z$ by $\beta$ regardless of whether the horse ran
a week or three years ago. If the true relationship saturates — the layoff
matters up to a point, after which more makes no difference — a linear term
cannot express it, and the standard remedy is to transform the feature
(a logarithm) or to bin it, both of which impose the shape in advance.

Piecewise-linear units express saturation directly: one unit switching off
above a threshold gives a slope that changes at a learned point.

## The race-conditional part, which is the sharpest difference

Consider a feature that is constant within a race — the going that day, the
class, the course, the field size. Call it $u_r$, the same for every runner
in race $r$.

In a linear score, such a feature contributes $\beta_u u_r$ to every runner's
score in that race. From the previous section, a per-race constant cancels
from every ratio in the likelihood. **A race-constant feature therefore
contributes nothing to a linear score.** Its coefficient is not identified,
and including the column adds no capacity at all.

The only way a linear model can use race-level information is through an
explicit interaction with a runner-level feature: a column such as
$u_r \times \text{draw}_{rj}$ does vary within the race and does survive the
cancellation. Again the interaction must be constructed by hand.

A network is not restricted in this way. Because $u_r$ enters the hidden
layers alongside the runner-level features, it can change the slope the
network applies to those features without contributing any additive constant
of its own. Race-level information becomes usable as a modifier of
runner-level effects, without an interaction column being specified.

This matters for reading paper 5's rung 1, where a network and a linear score
were given an identical feature set including a going term and four course
indicators — five columns that are constant within a race. On the linear side
those five columns can do nothing whatever; on the network side they can
modulate the remaining terms. Identical inputs, in this likelihood, do not
mean identical usable inputs.

## What the network does not buy

Two boundaries, since the section above could be read as claiming more than
it does.

The network does not obtain any dependence on the rest of the field. Weights
are shared and $f_\theta$ sees one runner's features, so $z_{rj}$ is still a
function of $x_{rj}$ alone, exactly as in the linear case. Making a runner's
score depend on the composition of the field requires a different
architecture — a permutation-invariant function of the whole race — which is
a change to the model class, not a consequence of adding hidden layers.

Nor does it buy anything on features that are genuinely uninformative. Extra
capacity applied to noise produces overfitting, which is what the validation
slice of section 2.5 exists to detect.

# Embeddings

## The construction

A categorical variable with $V$ levels — a trainer identifier, say — cannot
be fed to a network as an integer, since the arithmetic would imply an
ordering that does not exist. The standard treatments are one-hot encoding,
which represents level $v$ by a basis vector $e_v \in \mathbb{R}^V$, and an
embedding, which represents it by a learned vector.

An embedding is a matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}$ whose $v$-th row is
the representation of level $v$. The lookup is exactly the product $e_v^\top
E$, so an embedding is a linear layer applied to a one-hot vector, with the
multiplication implemented as an array index. Its rows are parameters and are
learned by the same gradient descent as every other weight: only the row for
level $v$ receives gradient from a row of data carrying that level.

## Why an embedding can carry more than a rate

A hand-built alternative is a summary statistic — for a trainer, the
proportion of prior runners that won. That is one number per level, fixed by
a formula chosen in advance.

An embedding is $d$ numbers per level, and their meaning is determined by the
objective. It can in principle encode that a trainer does well with
first-time-out sprinters and badly over longer distances, because the
embedding vector is concatenated with the other features before the
nonlinearity, and the network can therefore make its use of the other
features depend on which trainer this is. A single rate cannot express
anything conditional; it enters as one more additive term.

## The sample-size problem

The cost is parameters. The table holds $V \times d$ of them, and the row for
level $v$ is estimated only from rows carrying level $v$. Entity counts in
this kind of data are heavily skewed: a few trainers with thousands of
runners, a long tail with a handful each. A level appearing three times has a
$d$-vector fitted from three observations.

The standard remedy is a frequency threshold: levels with at least $n_{\min}$
rows in the fitting data get their own row, and everything below is pooled
into one shared bucket. This bounds the parameter count and prevents the
rarest levels from carrying essentially untrained vectors, at the cost that
all of them share one representation.

The vocabulary — which levels get their own row — must be fixed on the
fitting data alone. Deriving it from the data the model is evaluated on would
let that data determine the model's structure.

## The information-set point

There is a second difference between the two constructions, separate from
representational capacity, and it is the one paper 5's rung 2 examines.

An embedding row can only be learned from rows in the fitting sample. A
statistic computed by formula can be evaluated anywhere the underlying
records reach — including for levels that never appear in the fitting sample
at all, and using history from outside the modelled scope entirely.

Under a chronological split this asymmetry is not incidental. The evaluation
period is later than the fitting period and contains people and animals the
earlier period did not, and every one of them falls into the shared bucket.
The comparison between a learned embedding and a formula-based rate is
therefore a comparison between two information sets as much as between two
representations, and any reading of such a comparison has to account for
both.

# Sequence encoders

## The problem

The input is now a variable-length sequence $x_1, \ldots, x_T$ with each
$x_t \in \mathbb{R}^c$ — for paper 5, one vector per prior run of a horse,
with $c$ channels describing that run. The output must be a fixed-length
vector, because the scorer of section 3 takes a fixed-length input.

Averaging or summing the sequence produces a fixed-length vector but discards
order: it gives the same answer for a horse improving through its last five
runs and one declining through them.

## Recurrence

A recurrent network maintains a running state and updates it once per
element:

$$
h_t \;=\; \varphi\!\left(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b\right), \qquad h_0 = 0 .
$$

The final state $h_T$ is the summary. Order matters because $h_{t-1}$ enters
the update for $h_t$.

The difficulty is training. The gradient of the loss with respect to early
elements passes through $T$ successive multiplications by $U$ and by
derivatives of $\varphi$, so it tends to shrink or grow geometrically in $T$.
Long-range dependence is then hard to learn.

## The gated recurrent unit

The GRU addresses this with two gates. All quantities are vectors of the
hidden width $H$, $\odot$ is elementwise multiplication, and $\sigma$ is the
logistic function, so each gate is a vector of numbers in $(0,1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_t &= \sigma\!\left(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z\right)
&&\text{update gate} \\
r_t &= \sigma\!\left(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t-1} + b_r\right)
&&\text{reset gate} \\
\tilde{h}_t &= \tanh\!\left(W_h x_t + U_h \left(r_t \odot h_{t-1}\right)
+ b_h\right) &&\text{candidate state} \\
h_t &= \left(1 - z_t\right) \odot h_{t-1} \;+\; z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t
&&\text{new state}
\end{aligned}
$$

The last line is the substance. The new state is an interpolation between the
previous state and the candidate, controlled elementwise by $z_t$. Where
$z_t$ is near zero the corresponding coordinate of the state is carried
forward almost unchanged, which gives the gradient a near-identity path
across that step; where $z_t$ is near one the coordinate is replaced. The
network learns when to hold and when to overwrite, per coordinate, so
different hidden dimensions can operate over different spans of the sequence.

The reset gate controls how much of the previous state is visible when the
candidate is formed. With $r_t$ near zero the candidate depends on $x_t$
alone, which lets a coordinate discard accumulated history when the current
element is what matters.

Order changes the output, and not only in principle: $h_T$ is a function of
the sequence, and exchanging two elements changes it in general. This is the
property that distinguishes a recurrent summary from an average.

## Padding and masking

Batching requires a rectangular array, so sequences of different lengths must
be padded to a common width. Where the padding goes is not a free choice.

Suppose sequences are **left**-padded, with the real elements at the end, and
the summary is taken as the state after the final step. Feeding a zero vector
does not leave the state unchanged: with $x_t = 0$ the gates reduce to
$\sigma(U_z h_{t-1} + b_z)$ and so on, and the biases alone move the state
away from zero. The state entering the first real element then depends on how
many padded steps preceded it, so two horses with identical records but
different sequence lengths receive different summaries.

Two correct alternatives. Either mask the recurrence itself, copying
$h_{t-1}$ forward unchanged wherever the step is padding; or **right**-pad,
with the real elements first, and read the state at index $\text{len}$ rather
than at the end. Paper 5 takes the second. It is exact by construction: the
state at index $\text{len}$ is a function of the first $\text{len}$ inputs
and of nothing else, whatever the padded slots contain.

Two practical points follow. A row with no elements at all has no state to
read and should receive the zero vector explicitly. And the code used for an
unavailable reading must differ from the padding value: if $0$ is a
legitimate reading for a channel, padding with $0$ makes the two
indistinguishable to any check.

An index error here is quiet. Reading the state at $\text{len} \pm 1$ still
produces a summary that is invariant to padding width and content, and still
trains; it simply summarises the wrong element. Invariance tests alone do not
catch it. Comparing against the same encoder run on the unpadded sequence
does.

## Why a frozen encoder feeding a tree is weaker

A tempting arrangement is to obtain a sequence encoder some other way — train
it against a different objective, or leave it at its random initialisation —
freeze its parameters, and use its outputs as extra columns for a model that
is easier to fit, such as a gradient-boosted tree.

The representational comparison is exact. With the encoder frozen at
$E_{\text{fixed}}$, the composite model ranges over
$\{\, g \circ E_{\text{fixed}} : g \in \mathcal{G} \,\}$. With the encoder
trained jointly it ranges over
$\{\, g \circ E_\psi : g \in \mathcal{G}, \, \psi \in \Psi \,\}$, which
contains the first as the slice $\psi = \psi_{\text{fixed}}$. The joint model
can represent everything the frozen one can, and more.

The reason is the chain rule of section 2.2. When the encoder is trained
against the same loss, the gradient that reaches the scorer continues into
the encoder, and the encoder's parameters are adjusted to make its output
useful for that loss. Its coordinates come to mean something with respect to
the prediction. Freezing severs that path: the coordinates then mean whatever
the other procedure made them mean.

At the extreme of a random initialisation, the encoder is an arbitrary
nonlinear projection of the sequence. It will usually retain the information
— an arbitrary projection rarely destroys much — but its coordinates bear no
particular relation to the target, so the downstream model must recover the
relevant structure from an arbitrary basis, using the same finite data. An
encoder trained against a different objective is a milder version of the same
problem: an autoencoder, for instance, optimises reconstruction, and the
directions that reconstruct a run history well need not be the directions
that order horses well.

Two honest qualifications. "Weaker" here is a statement about the set of
representable functions, not a prediction about held-out performance: the
joint model has more parameters fitted on the same data and can generalise
worse. And the argument assumes the joint model is actually trainable, which
requires the differentiable chain of section 2.3 to be unbroken from the loss
through the scorer and into the encoder — which is exactly what the masking
arrangements above are there to preserve.
